introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Philosophy 2 (0790), Paper 2 (Philosophical Culture and Analysis), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2025. Duration: three hours.**

Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing at least one question from each section.

Each essay question shall be marked according to the following criteria:
- Coherence and organization of material;
- Clear presentation of the problematic;
- Identification and elaboration of the Thesis, Antithesis, Synthesis and Conclusion.

Each question carries 25 marks.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Règle de choix : la page de garde dit « answer FOUR questions, choosing at least one question from each section » (quatre questions au total, au moins une par section). `regles_choix` porte le minimum, une règle `parmi 1 sur 2` par section (Section One : questions 1-2 ; Section Two : questions 3-4 ; Section Three : questions 5-6) ; la règle « 4 questions en tout » n'est pas exprimable en entier et est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`. Le sujet ne dit pas si un candidat peut traiter les deux questions d'une même section.

Points : chaque question est imprimée « 25 marks » (4 x 25 = 100). Les critères de la page de garde (cohérence et organisation, présentation claire de la problématique, thèse, antithèse, synthèse et conclusion) s'appliquent aux dissertations (questions 1 à 4) sans barème chiffré par partie ; les questions de textes (5 et 6) ont leurs points par sous-question (Q5 : 5 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 25 ; Q6 : 5 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 25, où « 2x2 marks » est lu comme 4 points) : aucun écart de somme constaté, aucun point corrigé.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées de mémoire, sans accès à une source. Les auteurs et positions cités sont ceux de l'histoire de la philosophie établie, sans citation littérale, sans numéro de page et sans date précise (hors repères de siècle) ; à faire relire par un enseignant de philosophie avant mise en avant.

Sujet scanné (3 pages) avec filigrane gcerevision.com / Kawlo sans incidence sur la lecture ; aucune figure. Page de garde vérifiée : ADVANCED LEVEL, Philosophy 2, « Paper 2 (Philosophical Culture and Analysis) », code 0790, JUNE 2025, trois heures. L'intitulé du paper (« Philosophical Culture and Analysis ») et le mot « elaboration » dans les critères sont recopiés tels qu'imprimés (la session 2023 imprimait « Philosophical Writing and Analysis » et « development »).

Q3 : la référence à Hallen et Sodipo (étude des concepts yoruba de savoir et de croyance), à Oruka (philosophie des sages) et à la formule de Senghor sur le savoir intuitif est donnée en paraphrase prudente, sans titre d'ouvrage ni citation littérale.

questions.enonce_markdown:
African epistemology is basically traditional. Do you agree?

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction (problematic).** *Epistemology* is the theory of knowledge: what knowledge is, how it is acquired and how it is justified. *African epistemology* here means the ways in which African thinkers and peoples understand and justify knowledge. To call it "basically traditional" is to say that it rests on inherited, communal, oral beliefs and methods rather than on critical, individual, scientific inquiry. The problem is whether African epistemology is essentially of this kind, or whether this description is incomplete, partial or even a colonial stereotype.

**Thesis: yes, African epistemology is basically traditional.**
- *Communal and oral transmission.* In traditional societies knowledge is held and passed on by the community: elders, ancestors, proverbs, myths, initiation, storytelling. Truth is guaranteed by the authority of tradition and by the consensus of the group, as in the "unanimism" that Hountondji criticised.
- *Holistic and spiritual knowledge.* Mbiti and Tempels describe a world in which the visible and invisible are linked (living, ancestors, spirits, God). Knowledge is knowledge of this whole: to know is to participate in the vital order, not only to observe from outside. Senghor contrasted African intuitive and participatory knowing with Western analytical distance, though this contrast is much debated.
- *Sources of knowledge.* Besides sense experience and reason, traditional epistemologies accept testimony of elders and ancestors, divination, dreams, intuition and revelation. The knower is a member of a community, not an isolated individual.
- *Practical and moral orientation.* Knowledge serves life: farming, healing, social harmony, justice. It is bound to values (wisdom more than theory), which makes the epistemology fundamentally linked to culture and tradition.
- *Philosophers who describe it so.* The ethno-philosophers (Tempels, Kagame, Mbiti) and sage philosophy (Oruka) show that traditional communities have developed ideas about knowledge, belief and truth. Hallen and Sodipo's study of Yoruba concepts of knowledge and belief shows these ideas can be analysed.

**Antithesis: no, it is not basically, and not only, traditional.**
- *Critical traditions inside Africa.* Oruka's sage philosophy shows individual sages who question inherited beliefs. Wiredu insists that traditional thought contains superstition and authority-based beliefs which must be criticised, and that African philosophers must examine their own concepts with the tools of reason. Hountondji and Towa reject the idea that the collective beliefs of a people are philosophy.
- *Empirical and technical knowledge.* Traditional medicine, agriculture, metallurgy, navigation, architecture and astronomy involved observation, trial and correction, which is not mere inherited belief. African epistemology therefore includes empirical and rational elements.
- *The stereotype problem.* To call African knowledge "basically traditional" repeats the colonial view of the African as bound to custom and incapable of critical reason, as in the "prelogical" mentality of Lévy-Bruhl. Many Africans today practise and teach science, mathematics and philosophy in the same way as other peoples.
- *Change and plurality.* Africa is diverse, and its cultures have changed through contact with Islam, Christianity, colonialism and modern education. Modern African epistemology has to answer questions about science, technology and development, not only about ancestors.

**Synthesis.** African epistemology has traditional roots and many of its distinctive concepts (communal knowing, the link between the visible and invisible, the value of oral wisdom) come from them. But being rooted in tradition is not being confined to it. Wiredu's programme of critical conceptual analysis and conceptual "decolonisation", and Gyekye's view that traditions can be reflectively assessed and kept or changed, show a path: use tradition as a resource, submit it to criticism and open it to scientific knowledge.

**Conclusion.** The statement is partly right as a description of the origin and of much of the content of African epistemology, but wrong as a definition of its basic nature. African epistemology is both traditional and critical, local and universal; its quality lies in how tradition and critical reason are combined.
